content: Preformed crowns for primary molar teeth are available in various sizes and materials. These crowns are designed to cover decayed or developmentally defective teeth. They can be made entirely of stainless steel, referred to as preformed metal crowns (PMCs), or they may include a white veneer for improved aesthetics. Some crowns are also made entirely of white ceramic material. Typically, the placement of these crowns involves trimming the tooth and using local anesthesia. However, the Hall Technique allows PMCs to be placed without local anesthesia, carious tissue removal, or tooth preparation. Crowns are recommended for restoring primary molars that have undergone pulp treatment, are severely decayed, or are significantly damaged. Despite this, their use in clinical practice is limited. This review updates the original 2007 review and aims to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and safety of preformed crowns compared to conventional filling materials, other types of crowns, non-restorative caries treatment, or no treatment. It also explores whether the extent of decay affects the clinical outcomes of teeth restored with crowns versus fillings. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the effectiveness of crowns compared to fillings, other crown types, non-restorative approaches, or no treatment in children with untreated decay in primary molars. Trials comparing different methods of crown placement were also considered. To be included, studies had to report clinical outcomes at least six months after the intervention, except for outcomes like pain or discomfort during and immediately after treatment. Five studies were included in the review, evaluating three main comparisons. Four studies compared crowns with fillings. Two of these studies compared conventional PMCs with open sandwich restorations, while the other two compared PMCs placed using the Hall Technique with fillings. One of these studies also included a comparison of PMCs (Hall Technique) versus non-restorative caries treatment. In the two studies using conventional crown placement, all teeth had undergone pulpotomy before crown placement. The fifth study compared PMCs with aesthetic stainless steel crowns that had white veneers. No RCT evidence was found comparing different methods of fitting PMCs, such as the Hall Technique versus the conventional technique. For crowns versus fillings, all studies used PMCs. One study reported short-term outcomes and found no major failures or pain in either group. Moderate-quality evidence suggested that the risk of major failure was lower in the crowns group in the long term (risk ratio [RR] 0.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.06 to 0.56; 346 teeth in three studies). Similarly, moderate-quality evidence indicated that the risk of pain was lower in the crowns group in the long term (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.67; 312 teeth in two studies). Discomfort during the procedure was lower for crowns placed using the Hall Technique compared to fillings (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.87; 381 teeth). However, it is uncertain whether there is a clinically significant difference in the risk of gingival bleeding between crowns and fillings, either in the short term (RR 1.69, 95% CI 0.61 to 4.66; 226 teeth) or long term (RR 1.74, 95% CI 0.99 to 3.06; 195 teeth, two studies using PMCs with the conventional technique at 12 months). For crowns versus non-restorative caries treatment, only one study compared PMCs (Hall Technique) with non-restorative treatment. The evidence quality was very low, making the estimates uncertain. For metal crowns versus aesthetic crowns, one split-mouth study with 11 participants compared PMCs with aesthetic crowns (stainless steel with white veneers). The evidence quality was very low, and no conclusions could be drawn. In conclusion, crowns placed on primary molars with carious lesions or following pulp treatment are likely to reduce the risk of major failure or pain in the long term compared to fillings. Crowns placed using the Hall Technique may reduce discomfort during treatment compared to fillings. However, the evidence for crowns compared to non-restorative caries treatment and for metal versus aesthetic crowns is of very low quality. No RCTs have compared crowns placed conventionally versus using the Hall Technique.
